title: The eerie history of Colorado's Stanley Hotel
excerpt: Discover the history, mysteries and famous moments that helped turn The Stanley Hotel into one of the most haunted destinations in America.
content:
Oct. 20, 2026, 5:00 a.m. MT

At first glance, there's nothing particularly unsettling about The Stanley Hotel.

Perched above Estes Park, Colorado, the historic hotel has been drawing visitors for generations with its grand white architecture and sweeping mountain views.

Yet it's what people say happens inside that has helped shape its legacy. Decades of ghost stories, reported sightings and paranormal lore have turned the property into one of the most famous haunted hotels in America.

Before the ghost stories

The story begins in 1903, when inventor Freelan Oscar Stanley arrived in Estes Park hoping the mountain air would improve his health.

Captivated by the landscape, Stanley returned year after year before opening the hotel in 1909 as a luxury retreat that brought a touch of East Coast elegance to the Rocky Mountains, according to the hotel's website.

The property quickly became a centerpiece of Estes Park's growing mountain community. Its amenities were considered cutting-edge for the time, including electric lights, telephones, private bathrooms and a fleet of automobiles for guests.

The hotel that inspired 'The Shining'

More than six decades after The Stanley opened, one guest's visit would help seal the hotel's place in popular culture.

In 1974, horror author Stephen King and his wife, Tabitha King, stayed at the hotel near the end of the season as it prepared to close for the winter. The couple were the property's only guests that night, according to King's official website.

The quiet, nearly empty hotel left an impression. As King wandered the halls, he thought it seemed like "the perfect, maybe the archetypical, setting for a ghost story." That night, he dreamed of his young son running through the corridors while being chased by a fire hose.

After waking, King sat looking out at the Rocky Mountains and began piecing together the story that would become "The Shining."

"By the time the cigarette was done, I had the bones of the book firmly set in my mind," King wrote on his official website.

The novel was published in 1977, introducing readers to the fictional Overlook Hotel, an isolated mountain resort haunted by a sinister past. It went on to become one of King's most celebrated works, forever linking The Stanley to the story it helped inspire.

That connection grew further when "The Shining" was adapted into a major motion picture in 1980. Although The Stanley wasn't used as the filming location for the movie, many visitors still associate the hotel with King's fictional setting. With its grand architecture, long hallways and dramatic mountain backdrop, it's not hard to see why.

Room 217

Another chapter of the hotel's history began decades earlier in Room 217.

In 1911, chambermaid Elizabeth Wilson was injured in a gas explosion while staff were activating the hotel's backup lighting system. Wilson survived the blast and continued working at the hotel for years, but the incident eventually became one of the property's most enduring legends.

As the years passed, stories surrounding the room only added to its mystique. Guests have long shared accounts of unusual experiences there, helping make Room 217 one of the hotel's most sought-after accommodations, according to US Ghost Adventures, which researches haunted locations and local folklore.
